title: Circles and a Cricket Machine
subtitle: A Cambridge logician didn't invent overlapping circles — and said so. But he used them so well that his name stuck. He also built a machine that bowled out an Australian star.

card.essence: Draw a circle for each group. Where the circles overlap, things belong to both; outside them, things belong to neither. Every possible combination gets its own space.

intention: you'll learn the story of John Venn and his circles, use a Venn diagram to compare two options, and practise talking about what things share: both, either, neither, so do I, neither do I.
warmup: Think of a friend who is very different from you. What do you have in common?
When you compare two options — two jobs, two cities — how do you organise your thinking?
Do you remember drawing overlapping circles at school? What for?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The two courses overlap: both cover statistics, but only one includes programming.
items.meaning: overlap — to cover part of the same area or subject. (noun: an overlap between two things)

items.sent: As a logician, she was interested in what makes an argument valid.
items.meaning: logician — an expert in logic, the study of correct reasoning. (logic, logical, illogical)

items.sent: The app helps you visualise your spending, so you can see at a glance where the money goes.
items.meaning: visualise — to form a picture of something, in your mind or on paper. (noun visualisation; adj. visual)

items.sent: He resigned because the company's new direction was incompatible with his values.
items.meaning: incompatible — too different to exist or work together. (opposite compatible; incompatible with)

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: intersection · exclusive · category. Read each meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (adjective) Belonging to one group only; not shared.
items.meaning: exclusive — “The two options are mutually exclusive: you can't choose both.”

items.sent: (noun) A group of things that have something in common.
(noun) The place or set where two things cross or overlap.
items.meaning: intersection — “Her work sits at the intersection of art and science.” (also: a road junction)

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: have a lot in ___  ·  ___ ground  ·  ___ sense
items.meaning: common — shared. (have something in common, find common ground, common sense)

items.sent: ___ a resemblance to  ·  ___ in mind  ·  can't ___ it
items.meaning: bear — (bear a resemblance to = look like; bear in mind = remember; can't bear = hate)

items.sent: draw a ___  ·  reach a ___  ·  jump to ___s
items.meaning: conclusion — the judgement you reach after thinking. (verb conclude)

vocab_use: What do you and your best friend have in common? Where don't you overlap?
Name two things in your life that sometimes feel incompatible — work and family, sleep and a new baby?
When you think, do you visualise things, or think in words?

story.heading: Part 1 — A family of preachers
paras: John Venn was born in Hull, in the north of England, in 1834, into a family of evangelical churchmen. His grandfather, also called John Venn, had been rector of Clapham and a leader of the Clapham Sect, the group that campaigned against slavery. Everyone expected young John to become a priest too.

In 1853 he went to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and in 1857 he graduated as sixth Wrangler — sixth among the best mathematics students of his year. Two years later he was ordained as a priest.

But in 1862 he returned to Cambridge to teach moral sciences — subjects that included logic and probability. Teaching changed the direction of his life. He needed ways to make difficult arguments clear to his students.
checks: What did his family expect him to become?
Why did he return to Cambridge in 1862?
answers: He was ranked sixth among the best mathematics students of his year.
To teach moral sciences, including logic and probability.
story.discuss: Have you ever followed a path that other people expected, and then changed direction?

story.heading: Part 2 — Circles that were not new
paras: In July 1880, Venn published a paper with a long title: “On the Diagrammatic and Mechanical Representation of Propositions and Reasonings”. In it, he used overlapping circles to show logical statements. With three circles, every possible combination — in A and B but not C, in all three, in none — has its own space.

He never claimed the idea was his own. Circles had been used for logic before, most famously by the mathematician Leonhard Euler in his Letters to a German Princess of 1768, and Venn called his diagrams “Eulerian circles”. He later wrote: “Of course the device was not new then, but it was so obviously representative of the way in which any one, who approached the subject from the mathematical side, would attempt to visualise propositions, that it was forced upon me almost at once.”
What Venn added was a system: his diagrams show every possible overlap, even the empty ones. The name “Venn diagram” came later; the philosopher Clarence Irving Lewis used it in 1918.
checks: When did Venn publish his paper?
What did Venn call his diagrams?
What did Venn add to the older circles?
answers: A system that shows every possible overlap, even the empty ones.
story.discuss: Is it fair that the diagram carries Venn's name, not Euler's?

story.heading: Part 3 — The machine that bowled a star
paras: In 1883 Venn left the clergy, having concluded that his beliefs were incompatible with the Church of England. In the same year he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. Later in life he turned to history, and with his son compiled an enormous register of past members of the university.

He also had a rare talent for building machines. One of them bowled cricket balls. When the Australian team visited Cambridge in 1909, the machine reportedly bowled out one of their star batsmen, Victor Trumper. In 2024, the university's engineering department built a new version of it.

Venn died in 1923. Today he is remembered in a stained-glass window at his old college, on a bridge in Hull, and in almost every classroom in the world. Not bad for a man who borrowed his most famous idea — and was honest enough to say so.
checks: Why did Venn leave the clergy?
What happened when the Australian team visited Cambridge?
Give two ways Venn is remembered today.
answers: He concluded that his beliefs were incompatible with the Church of England.
His bowling machine reportedly bowled out their star batsman, Victor Trumper.
Any two: a stained-glass window at his college, a bridge in Hull, Venn diagrams in classrooms.
story.discuss: Why do some people become famous for ideas they didn't invent?

tool_tab.lead: Each circle is a group. Where the circles overlap, things belong to both groups; outside the circles are things that belong to neither. Here, two job offers are compared.

diagram.outside: outside both circles: company car (neither offers it)

how: Choose what you are comparing — two or three things — and draw one circle for each.
Put features that only one thing has in its own part of its circle.
Put shared features in the overlap. With three circles, check every overlap, including the middle.
Read the picture: is the overlap big or small? Are the differences the ones that matter to you?

sort.intro: Two friends are choosing a holiday: the mountains or the coast. Where on the diagram does each feature go?

items.why: both places have it — the overlap.
neither place has one — outside both circles.

items.text: Fresh seafood restaurants by the harbour.
items.why: only the coast has a harbour.

breaks: Size isn't shown. A big area on the page might hold two tiny features; a Venn diagram doesn't measure importance.
Too many circles. Beyond three, the diagram quickly becomes hard to read.
Things aren't always in or out. Real categories are fuzzy: is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable?
discuss: Draw a Venn diagram of you and someone you know. What surprised you?
When is a list of pros and cons better than a Venn diagram?

cousins.name: Ikigai
cousins.text: Four overlapping circles: what you love, what you're good at, what the world needs and what you can be paid for.

cousins.name: The Mind Map

cousins.name: SWOT Analysis

cousins.text: Two questions, four boxes — another picture of what's shared and what's hidden.

grammar.name: both, either, neither — and so do I
grammar.lead: Venn diagrams are about what things share. English has a small family of words for exactly that — and a quick way to say “me too” and “me neither”.
notes:
both … and — two things together; both of + us / them / the …
“Both the hotel and the flat have a pool.”  “Both of them speak French.”

either … or — one or the other; neither … nor — not one and not the other.
“We can meet either on Monday or on Friday.”  “Neither the bus nor the train goes there.”

either of / neither of + plural noun — usually with a singular verb in careful English.
“Neither of the plans is perfect.”

so / neither + auxiliary + subject — for agreeing.
“I love jazz.” — “So do I.”  “I can't swim.” — “Neither can I.”  “She went to Rome.” — “So did we.”
Watch out: no double negative: ~~Neither of them didn't come~~ → “Neither of them came.”

items: 1. ___ my brother and my sister live abroad.
2. You can pay ___ by card ___ in cash.
3. ___ of the two jobs offers a company car.
4. The flat is neither cheap ___ close to the station.
5. ___ of my parents was born here — they're both from Poland.

exercises.heading: Agree with the speaker
items: 4. “I'm going to compare the two offers tonight.” → ___

grammar.closing: Now compare yourself with your teacher: find two things you both like and one thing neither of you does — and react with So do I / Neither do I.

speak.intro: Draw circles out loud. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “Both of them …” · “Neither of them …” · “That goes in the overlap.” · “So do I / Neither do I.”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Two choices
paras: Compare two options you are thinking about — two jobs, two phones, two places to live. What is unique to each, and what do they share?

tasks.label: Task 2 — Three circles
paras: Draw three circles for three people in your life. What sits in the middle — the thing all three share?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Borrowed fame
paras: Venn made a borrowed idea famous. Tell the story of someone else who became famous for an idea that wasn't completely new.

final: Is it more interesting to find what people share, or how they differ?
Venn was open about borrowing his idea. Why are many people less honest?
Can a simple diagram ever capture a complicated decision?
From memory: compare Venn and Euler in four sentences using both, neither, either and so did.
